newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian president resigns, new parliament meets.
newsitem.headline: Albanian president resigns, new parliament meets.

text.p: Albania's discredited president Sali Berisha resigned on Wednesday to join the opposition in the new parliament, which met for the first time surrounded by armed police.

The session opened with a minute's silence for the more than 1,500 people killed in unrest that began in March after the collapse of pyramid investment schemes, which Berisha conceded his government did too little to control.

"It is up to this parliament and all political forces to think deeply about what happened in Albania, to take into consideration the interests of our people to resolve the political, economic, social, moral and national problems," said Socialist deputy Dritero Agolli, who opened the session in his capacity as one of the assembly's 10 oldest members.
In a letter to the legislature, Berisha said he had stepped down to take a seat as an opposition deputy for his Democratic Party, which suffered a resounding defeat in June 29 elections.
"I declare today my irrevocable resignation from the post of head of state to continue political parliamentary life supporting the values and the alternative I believe in," Berisha said.

The news was greeted with celebratory gunshots in Tirana and in anti-Berisha strongholds like Berat and the southern port of Vlore, the flashpoint of protests in March over the collapse of shady pyramid investment schemes.
Western diplomats including the U.S. ambassador, who stayed away from the opening of the parliament elected in disputed elections last year, attended Wednesday's session.

A million weapons have been looted from armouries since February and security at the parliament was tight, with armed police including plainclothes officers ringing the building and an armoured personnel carrier parked nearby.

Berisha's government resigned in March, and was replaced by a Socialist-led national unity administration. The new assembly inherits the task of restoring law and order and resolving the economic chaos left by the collapse of the pyramid schemes.

Democratic Party deputies apart from secretary-general Genc Pollo boycotted the session to protest at the conduct of the elections, which were described by international monitors as acceptable, if far from perfect.

Agolli refused Pollo permission to speak, saying the institutions of the parliament were still not elected. A commission must verify the mandate of each deputy, and the plenary session continues on Thursday.
Parliament is expected to elect Socialist Party secretary general Rexhep Mejdani as president to replace Berisha.
Following constitutional court rulings on disputes and some changing of alliances, the Socialists and their coalition allies will have 118 seats and the Democrats 24 in the 155-seat parliament.
The new assembly was dubbed the "parliament of Kalashnikovs", a reference to assault rifles, by pro-Berisha newspapers on Wednesday, and "the parliament of hope" by pro-Socialist dailies.
Koha Jone's front page had a photograph of a wild-eyed Berisha giving a stiff-armed Hitler salute to a rally with the headline "July 23, 1997 - The end of the dictatorships".

Berisha, a former heart surgeon and communist, was initially praised in the West for rapidly introducing market reforms but enthusiasm faded as he resorted to increasingly authoritarian methods and failed to check the spread of the pyramid schemes.

Democracy has only shaky foundations in Albania, where Stalinist leader Enver Hoxha ruled with an iron fist for 40 years until his death in April 1985, crushing opposition and isolating his state under a policy of self-reliance.
His successor, communist President Ramiz Alia, ruled out change but anti-government demonstrations from July 1990 led to reforms, culminating in multi-party elections in March 1991.
